title: Direct Preference Optimization from ratios to gradients

key_terms.DPO: Direct Preference Optimization, which fits a policy to preferences with loss -log sigma(beta m) using a frozen reference.
key_terms.Implicit reward: The scaled log ratio of policy to reference probability for a response, whose context constant cancels in comparisons.
key_terms.Log-ratio margin: The chosen-response log ratio minus the rejected-response log ratio, zero when policy equals reference.
key_terms.Beta parameter: The strength of the implied KL regularization, which scales the margin inside the logistic loss.

outcome: Derive the DPO loss from a regularized preference model and distinguish sequence log probabilities, temperature effects and held-out evaluation.
verification: At the reference policy the loss is log 2 with derivative -1, the preferred-action probabilities for the three beta values are 0.9, 0.75 and about 0.634, and the sequence-sum and mean-token margins have opposite signs.

exercises.title: Evaluate the reference
exercises.task: Set policy and reference log odds equal for any positive beta.
exercises.expected: The loss for a positive preference is log 2.
exercises.answer: The initial classifier is indifferent under the pairwise parameterization.

reasoning.approach: Call `dpo_loss(3, 3, 0.1)`. The policy and reference log-odds shifts are equal, so z = beta times (3 - 3) = 0.
reasoning.why: With z = 0 the loss is `logaddexp(0, 0)` = log 2. At initialization, when the policy equals the reference, every preference pair costs log 2 regardless of beta.
reasoning.pitfall: Expecting the initial loss to depend on beta is the mistake. Beta scales the margin, and a zero margin scaled by anything is still zero.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts `np.isclose(dpo_loss(3, 3, 0.1), np.log(2))`, and case A asserts the same for beta 2.

exercises.title: Differentiate the two-action loss
exercises.task: Use beta 2 and zero reference-relative log-odds shift.
exercises.answer: The result includes the beta scale and the logistic residual; it should agree with finite differences.

reasoning.approach: Call `dpo_gradient(0, 0, 2)`. The formula is beta times (sigmoid(z) - win_fraction).
reasoning.why: With z = 0 the sigmoid is 0.5 and the win fraction is 1, so the derivative is 2 times (0.5 - 1) = -1. Case A confirms this at delta 0.4 against a central finite difference.
reasoning.pitfall: Dropping the beta factor gives -0.5. That is the gradient with respect to z, not delta, and it would understate the step size by a factor of beta.
reasoning.verify: Case A asserts `dpo_gradient(0, 0, 2) == -1` and `np.isclose(numeric, dpo_gradient(delta, 0, 2), atol=1e-10)`.

exercises.title: Compare beta optima
exercises.task: Fit a 3:1 preference ratio with beta 0.5, 1 and 2 under a uniform reference.
exercises.hint: The optimum policy-logit shift is log 3 divided by beta.
exercises.answer: Initial gradient magnitude and final optimum displacement are different properties of the objective.

reasoning.approach: Call `fitted_delta(3, 1, beta)` for beta 0.5, 1 and 2, then take the sigmoid of each.
reasoning.why: The optimum is delta = log(3) / beta. For beta 0.5, delta = log 9 and the sigmoid is 9 / 10 = 0.9. For beta 1, it is 0.75. For beta 2, delta = log of the square root of 3 and the probability is about 0.634. At each optimum, beta times delta equals log 3, so the gradient is zero.
reasoning.pitfall: Assuming a larger beta moves the policy further because its initial gradient is larger is the mistake. Larger beta gives larger first steps but a smaller final change from the reference.
reasoning.verify: Case B asserts probabilities `[0.9, 0.75, np.sqrt(3) / (1 + np.sqrt(3))]` and gradients below 1e-12 at each optimum.

exercises.title: Change length normalization
exercises.task: Use the token log-ratio arrays in the reference exercise.
exercises.expected: The sequence-sum margin is negative while the mean-token margin is positive.
exercises.hint: Chosen and rejected sequences have different lengths.
exercises.answer: Normalizing each sequence by its own length changes its relative contribution and therefore the objective.

reasoning.approach: Compute per-token log-ratios: chosen is [0.3, 0.3] (two tokens) and rejected is [0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2] (four tokens). Compare sums and means.
reasoning.why: The chosen sum is 0.6 and the rejected sum is 0.8, a margin of -0.2. The chosen mean is 0.3 and the rejected mean is 0.2, a margin of +0.1. The longer rejected response wins on sums because it has more tokens.
reasoning.pitfall: Assuming normalization is a minor detail is the mistake. Summing favors longer sequences, averaging removes that effect, and each defines a different objective.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts `chosen.sum() - rejected.sum() < 0` and `chosen.mean() - rejected.mean() > 0`.

exercises.title: Protect the reference
exercises.task: Update the reference parameters while retaining the same loss label.
exercises.hint: The reference is part of the training specification.
exercises.answer: Reference refresh can be a deliberate algorithmic choice, but it is not the same fixed-reference DPO problem.

reasoning.approach: Keep the reference model frozen for the whole run. If it is updated, record that as a different algorithm.
reasoning.why: The DPO loss measures the policy relative to the reference. If the reference moves, the same loss value refers to a different comparison point, and the fixed-reference optimum from exercise 3 no longer applies.
reasoning.pitfall: Letting the reference share parameters with the policy, for example by not copying it, is a common bug. The loss then goes to log 2 every step and training appears stuck.
reasoning.verify: No reference assertion covers this task. Hash the reference parameters before and after training and confirm they are identical.

exercises.title: Bound the claim
exercises.task: Observe a lower training DPO loss.
exercises.expected: Conclude improved fit to the declared preference objective only.
exercises.hint: Separate training labels from independent task outcomes.
exercises.answer: Task utility, robustness, calibration and critical constraints still need their own held-out evaluation.

reasoning.approach: State that a lower training DPO loss shows the policy fits the training preference pairs better under the declared beta and reference.
reasoning.why: The loss rewards matching the labeled preferences. It does not measure whether answers are correct, robust to new prompts, calibrated or free of critical errors.
reasoning.pitfall: Reporting the lower loss as an improved model is the mistake. Eval-019 shows a policy can raise a proxy while lowering true utility.
reasoning.verify: Pair the training loss with held-out preference accuracy and an independent task metric, as in the decision gates of eval-016.
